description: Ground truth for the flaky-test research artifacts. Categories follow FlakeBench (Rahman, Dutta, Shi - OOPSLA 2025): async, concurrency, time, uc, od, non-flaky.

measurement.method: fresh JVM per run via org.junit.runner.JUnitCore, class-level granularity
measurement.note: Failure rates are machine- and load-dependent and drift between sessions. The invariant that matters is that each labelled test has been observed to both pass and fail on the same code.
measurement.originalOrder: Surefire runOrder is pinned to alphabetical in the root pom. Every OD test is written to pass in that order: each victim's class sorts ahead of its polluter, and the state-setter sorts ahead of its brittle.
measurement.odNote: OD failure counts are out of 25 shuffled class orders (seed 11), not out of repeated runs of one order. Unlike the async and concurrency rates these are deterministic given the order: each has been confirmed by an explicit two-class probe showing the victim passes alone and fails directly after its polluter.
measurement.ucNote: Unordered-collection order is only nondeterministic here because the standings are allocated across threads. Measured directly with tools/HashOrderProbe: a HashMap keyed by player id iterates identically on every JVM run, since String hash codes are fixed by the language, and even an identity-hashed HashSet is stable when it is filled on one thread. Spreading the allocation over a worker per venue is what moves it, with the contents still complete.
measurement.timeNote: Timing budgets were set from tools/TimingProbe rather than chosen: export costs a mean of 0.5-0.9ms with an 8-11ms tail, render 0.03ms. Budgets sit inside that band, which is what makes the assertions flaky rather than always-passing or always-failing.

flakesync.note: Primary FlakeSync target. Mirrors Figure 1 of the ICSE'24 paper: submit async work, sleep a fixed time, assert on shared state.
flakesync.observedResult: Repairable, confirmed by applying the patch. The barrier location matches ground truth (LiveScoreIngestTest#105, immediately before the assertEquals). The critical point does not: FlakeSync converged on WorkerPool.beforeExecute, the pool-wide dispatch hook, rather than the expected ScorecardUpdater.onBall. deltadebug minimized 53 locations to WorkerPool#59, a choke point that starves every task, and critsearch explored outward from there. The repair is correct and the barrier threshold, once fixed, is exactly the delivery count.
flakesync.patchThresholdBug: The emitted patch was broken as generated and had to be corrected by one constant. barrierpointsearch measured a threshold of 240 - 120 warmup tasks from primePipeline() plus 120 from the test - but the patch inserts WorkerPool.resetExecutions() at the start of the test method, after @Before has already run the warmup. Only the test's own 120 tasks can therefore ever be counted, so the barrier 'while (getExecutedStatus() < 240) Thread.yield()' spins forever. Confirmed with jstack: main parked in Thread.yield() at the barrier line, still spinning after 180s. Threshold corrected 240 -> DELIVERIES (120); the test then passed 10/10 in isolation and 50/50 under rerun.py.

tests.settleConstant: Uses its own ISOLATED_SETTLE_MILLIS = 100 rather than the SETTLE_MILLIS = 3 shared by the other LiveScoreIngestTest methods. FlakeSync always invokes a single test method, which leaves the pipeline far colder than the suite (tools/Calibrate: ~30ms first ingest, ~5ms second, warm band 1.3-2.5ms), so at 3ms the delay-0 baseline failed 5/5 in isolation and every injected delay would have looked equally guilty. Calibrated to the smallest value giving a clean baseline under the plugin instrumentation. See Running_FlakeSync.md.
tests.flakinessNote: Repaired: FlakeSync's generated barrier has been applied, so the test now blocks until all 120 ingest tasks have run instead of sleeping a fixed time. 0 failures in 50 runs. It was 8/50 with SETTLE_MILLIS and 0/50 with ISOLATED_SETTLE_MILLIS before the barrier. No longer an async-wait flaky test: it synchronises on a real condition, which is the repair the ICSE-24 paper is about.

tests.note: Sleeps SETTLE_MILLIS - 1 (2ms) and asserts on ScorecardUpdater.appliedCount(), the same async-wait shape as its siblings. Was absent from this file until it turned up at 43/50 in a rerun.py measurement; the omission was a labelling gap, not a deliberate exclusion. It has the tightest wait of the five sleeping methods in the class, which is why it fails most often.

flakesync.note: Exercises FlakeSync's multi-execution threshold path: the critical point must run many times (once per milestone) before the barrier may proceed, so a single-execution barrier is not sufficient.

tests.note: Passed 50/50 in isolation but failed in the full Maven suite, where the JVM is shared with ~700 other tests. Flaky only under suite conditions.

flakesync.note: Deliberate negative control. The ICSE'24 paper states FlakeSync cannot repair 'exact timing' tests: the assertion is on elapsed wall-clock time, so no barrier makes it deterministic. A repair reported here would be a false positive.

adversarial.hypothesis: FlakyLens (OOPSLA'25) reports that its classifiers key on surface tokens rather than semantics, losing up to 18.37pp F1 under perturbation. These two groups test that directly on unperturbed, naturally written tests.

flakyWithoutTokens.note: Genuinely async-flaky. Every wait is behind a domain-named helper on the MatchDay fixture -- day.drinks(), day.tea() -- so the method body contains none of sleep, Thread, await, latch, concurrent, Executor, timeout, Duration, Atomic or millis. Verified by token scan.

nonFlakyWithTokens.note: Deterministic: every assertion follows an explicit awaitIdle, and every shared structure is a concurrent one. Bodies carry 4 to 8 flakiness tokens each. 40/40 passes.

adversarial.tokenScan: verified with tools/extract_tests.py plus the token list in the report
